source.title: Sketch-Based Empirical Natural Gradient Methods for Deep Learning
source.authors: Minghan Yang; Dong Xu; Zai-Wen Wen; Mengyun Chen; Peng-Xiang Xu

record.file_problem: The supplied full text is present. Its displayed title says “Sketchy Empirical Natural Gradient Methods for Deep Learning,” while the supplied title field says “Sketch-Based Empirical Natural Gradient Methods for Deep Learning.”
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests large-batch training and reports that SENG reaches the same ImageNet test-accuracy target at batch size 4096 within the same 41 epochs as at smaller batch sizes, qualifying the claim that large batches necessarily hurt under a fixed epoch budget. The optimizer comparisons otherwise focus on training time and do not test the mapped generalization claims.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s own ImageNet large-batch experiment, including each separately reported batch size, and optimizer comparisons on other datasets where the report gives threshold-reaching times and explicit non-attainment. The latter outcomes concern whether a method reaches a stated test-accuracy target, not a controlled comparison of train-test generalization gaps; they are not mapped to V4. Cited prior work on generalization gaps is not recorded as this study’s result.
record.test_reason: The study compares Adam and momentum SGD on held-out accuracy, including explicit best accuracies when targets are missed (V4), and compares SENG batch sizes on attainment of the same accuracy within 41 epochs (V5). Neither version requires a measured train-test gap. The optimizer tuning extends beyond learning rates and schedules, and the large-batch recipes change with batch size.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors conclude that SENG is competitive with SGD and KFAC and scales promisingly. They also explicitly interpret reaching 75.9% at batch 4096 within the same 41 epochs as evidence of large-batch effectiveness. They do not establish equality of final accuracy or train-test gaps.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes and evaluates sketchy empirical natural gradient (SENG), comparing it with SGD, Adam and KFAC; it does not reproduce the original studies’ methods for memorization, width, architecture bias, optimizer generalization, regularization, sharpness, or memorized-example removal. Its large-batch experiment uses SENG on ResNet50/ImageNet-1k and reports test-accuracy target attainment and scaling efficiency.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size and GPU count change reported total training time and time per epoch; the paper states all four batch sizes attain the same 75.9% test-accuracy target within 41 epochs. Matrix-update frequency changes reported training time and epochs to the target in Table 8.

fits_no_version.finding: SENG and KFAC differ in elapsed time and per-epoch cost to reach accuracy targets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sketching empirical natural-gradient computations can reduce time to target relative to the tested KFAC implementation.

fits_no_version.finding: At batch 256, SENG reaches 75.9% ImageNet accuracy in 41 epochs, SGD in 76 and KFAC in 42.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice changes epochs and elapsed time needed to reach a specified ImageNet accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing batch size and GPU count substantially reduces SENG training time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distributed SENG provides approximately 90–93% reported scaling efficiency over the tested hardware configurations.

record.problems: The experiments report test accuracy, training accuracy and training loss in curves, but do not quantify train-test error gaps or compare memorization/generalization. Table 3 reports time and target attainment for SENG across batch sizes without a small-batch optimizer baseline at the same fixed epoch budget. Results in Table 4 are averages of three runs without a stated uncertainty measure; Table 4 layout is flattened in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows were omitted. Figure 1, Figure 2 and Figure 3 show performance curves, but the supplied text does not provide recoverable point values for separate conditions; Table 4 and Table 5 provide the extracted numeric outcomes.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Held-out error as width increases beyond interpolation; the wide-network theorem concerns training-loss convergence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.

The restriction to tuning only learning rates and schedules; equal or better Adam training performance; language benchmarks; switching optimizers and decoupled weight decay. Adam beta parameters and weight decay are also tuned here.

An unchanged-recipe batch-size penalty; the critical batch-size threshold; matched final accuracies after a common full training budget; longer-training remedies; language models; and causal isolation of individual recipe adaptations.
Dropout addition, removal, underfitting and small-dataset effects.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and rankings of generalization gaps.
Removal of memorized examples versus random removal.

record.verdict_notes: The record incorrectly excludes V4 merely because the experiments emphasize time to target: explicit best held-out accuracies and target attainment establish optimizer rankings. Conversely, the V5 result uses changing recipes (Table 7), so it supports the adaptation clause rather than contradicting the qualified version. The study is not an original source for these versions. Conclusions use only the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of fixed random labels and natural-label test performance.
Test error as network width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance and train-test generalization gaps. The paper compares optimizers for time to test-accuracy thresholds, not the version’s stated outcome.

Only ImageNet ResNet50 with SENG is tested at multiple batch sizes; the paper does not test the stated classifier and language-model scope, smaller-batch generalization-gap comparisons, or recipe adaptations against a matched fixed-epoch baseline.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other measures of the train-test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.

relationships.condition: VGG16 bn on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100; ResNet18 on CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and SVHN, with broader hyperparameter tuning
relationships.reason: Adam has worse held-out accuracy than momentum SGD in R5, R6, R8, R9 and R10, even though tuning also includes weight decay and Adam beta parameters.
relationships.display_finding: Reported held-out accuracy favored momentum SGD despite searches over weight decay and Adam beta parameters, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: VGG16 bn on SVHN with broader hyperparameter tuning
relationships.reason: R7 reverses the optimizer ranking: Adam reaches 94.97% best test accuracy versus SGD's 75.5%, showing that the disadvantage is workload dependent.
relationships.display_finding: Reported best test accuracy is 94.97% for Adam versus 75.5% for SGD, but this comparison remains unverified.

relationships.condition: ResNet50/ImageNet with SENG and batch-specific learning-rate, warmup, damping and schedule settings
relationships.reason: R1–R4 all reach the 75.9% target in 41 epochs at batches 512–4096, supporting V5's allowance for adapted recipes to avoid a penalty at a common epoch budget.
relationships.display_finding: Unverified results suggest the adapted SENG recipes reached the same accuracy target within a common epoch budget.
